abstract: Artificial intelligence models for echocardiography interpret studies without identifying the structures that support their outputs. We show that this spatial grounding does not emerge from the pretraining of current vision-language models. General-purpose and medical vision-language models and an open-vocabulary detector recalled 3% or fewer of cardiac structures and scored below a box that never sees the image. EchoLens, a detector trained on 5,912 expert-annotated structures and 4,219 Doppler signals from 136 patients, recalled 87% and localized structures as reliably as a blinded expert reader (box centre within the reference in 95.7% and 95.3% of cases). It covers 21 structures across 11 transthoracic views and 11 spectral Doppler signal types. In external data, two physicians judged 81-92% of its detections correct across all 11 views, and it identified the Doppler signal type in 83% of frames. EchoLens provides the spatial layer that grounded echocardiographic interpretation requires.
hook: An echo-specific detector finds 87% of heart structures where general AI models find 3% or fewer.
summary: General and medical vision-language models could not point to cardiac structures in ultrasound, so the authors trained EchoLens on expert-annotated structures and Doppler signals from 136 patients. It matched a blinded expert reader on box placement across 21 structures and 11 views. Limit: training came from a small patient set and external checks used two physician judges.
title: Expert-level localization of fine-grained cardiac structures across the transthoracic echocardiogram
